newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama's president signs homeland for Indian group.
newsitem.headline: Panama's president signs homeland for Indian group.

text.p: Panamanian President Ernesto Perez Balladares signed into law on Friday an autonomous homeland for the nation's largest Indian group.
Leaders of the Ngobe-Bugle Indians, numbering 125,000, the largest of six Indian groups, have been pressing for an Indian territory for 25 years.

"Now Indian people can be sure that no one can snatch away what belongs to them. Now they can be sure that no one will threaten their religious beliefs, language or customs," Perez Balladares said at a ceremony in Canquintu, some 300 miles (500 km) from Panama City.

Although Indian activist Marcelino Moctezuma said the territory "finally puts an end to centuries of invasion," others were upset that the 1.72 million-acre (700,000-hectare) homeland included a project to mine the world's 12th largest copper deposit.
"On one hand it's great to finally achieve this, but on the other hand we have this mining project and I'm against it," said Diana Ellington, an Ngobe-Bugle Indian who attended the ceremony.
Canadian mining company Tiomin Resources Inc plans to go ahead with its project to mine a copper deposit in Cerro Colorado in Chiriqui province.
